cards.text: Jesus is still answering His disciples, who asked when the temple would fall and what the sign would be (Luke 21:7). He's just told them Jerusalem will be surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). Now He speaks of signs in the sun and moon and stars, and of dismay among the nations down on the earth.

cards.question: Down on the earth, what does Jesus say has the nations bewildered?

cards.text: Then Jesus says men will faint from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth. Friend, I nearly fainted every time that junk drawer rattled open, and it was always just somebody hunting for tape.

cards.question: Jesus says men will faint because the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

cards.text: And now comes the moment all of this has been building to. At that time, Jesus says, they will see someone coming in a cloud with power and great glory.

cards.question: Who does Jesus say they will see coming in a cloud with power and great glory?

cards.text: Friend, the Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Luke 19:10). Then He tells His listeners what to do when these things begin to happen.

cards.question: When these things begin to happen, what does Jesus tell His listeners to do?

answers.text: Stand up and lift up your heads
Kneel down and cover your faces
Sit still and close your eyes

cards.question: Jesus tells them to lift up their heads, because their ___ is drawing near.

cards.text: Then Jesus tells them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees.

cards.question: In Jesus' parable, when the trees sprout leaves, what can you see for yourself is near?
So also, Jesus says, when you see these things happening, know that the ___ of God is near.

cards.text: Then Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.

cards.question: Jesus sets heaven and earth beside His own words. Which does He say will never pass away?
Jesus says heaven and earth will pass away.

cards.text: Then Jesus turns it into a warning: watch yourselves. He says their hearts could get weighed down.

cards.question: What does Jesus name among the things that can weigh their hearts down?
If their hearts get weighed down, how does Jesus say that day will come upon them?
Jesus says the day He's warning about will come only on the people of Jerusalem.

cards.text: So Jesus says to keep watch at ALL times, and pray. Friend, that is the exact opposite of the snooze button.

cards.question: Jesus tells them to pray for the ___ to escape all that is about to happen, and to ___ before the Son of Man.

cards.text: That's where Jesus' sermon ends. And every day, Jesus teaches at the temple.

cards.question: Jesus teaches at the temple every day. Where does He go out to spend the night every evening?
Early in the morning, all the people would come to hear Jesus at the temple.

findings.problem: The card says His disciples asked the question in Luke 21:7. In the BSB, 21:5 says 'some of them' were remarking about the temple, and 21:7 says only 'they asked Him.' Luke doesn't name the askers as disciples, so the card fills in who is speaking. A safer wording is 'Jesus is still answering the question about when the temple would fall and what the sign would be (Luke 21:7).'

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card is only a bare quote of Luke 21:29 with no Papa Dorin voice and no context. It doesn't set up that a parable is a picture from everyday life, and it doesn't lead into the question about what the leaves show. The card reads as stripped down.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The card is only a bare quote of Luke 21:32 with no Papa Dorin voice and no storyteller line to carry the moment. Together with card 1, it leaves the whole parable stop without his personality.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The walkthrough has only two jokes in three stops: the junk-drawer fainting line in stop 1 card 3 and the snooze-button line in stop 3 card 5. Stop 1 cards 1, 5 and 7 and both story cards in stop 2 read as plain, pleasant narration. There are moments that could hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, like the leaves telling you summer is coming or a trap springing suddenly. Papa Dorin doesn't come through as laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
